summary: The agent (Claude Opus, reasoning effort max) spent about 30 minutes and 35 turns reading the buggy dispatch tool and data files, then rewrote planner/optimize.py, plant.py, tariff.py and data.py, correctly diagnosing and fixing several of the planted bugs: net-to-gross CV conversion, missing engine start costs/day-ahead optimization, UTC/local weather matching, weekday-from-UTC tariff bug, the ignored middle part-load point, intercooler heat miscounted as recoverable HT heat, cooling-tower load undercounting chiller compressor work and absorber driving heat, the kVA limit ignoring generator reactive support, and outages being applied only to engines. This fixed the visible day and produced a near-correct plan on several hidden days (39/55 sub-tests passed, including a full pass on the visible day). However, the agent explicitly and knowingly declined to implement the condenser-water-temperature trade-off (running the absorption chiller with the tower header held at its 22°C floor on cool days) that the task author identifies as the central coupling bug; it reasoned (incorrectly) that the plan format had no field to record which mode was used. This single omission cascades into the two biggest failures: day h2 has units running outside availability, and day h3 crashes outright (RuntimeError: no loading of the plant meets demand at 13:30) because without the absorption chiller as the engines' heat sink on a cool spring day, no feasible dispatch exists. Days h1 and h4 pass all balance/limit checks but miss the least-cost test by 10-12% (cost ~7,144 vs best 6,403; ~7,754 vs best 7,268) and fail the connection kVA limit by a similar margin, indicating a remaining suboptimality or constraint-handling gap beyond the acknowledged omission. Final reward was 0.0 (6 failed, 10 errored due to h3's crash, 39 passed) out of 55 sub-tests across 5 days.

task_specification.explanation: instruction.md (and the fuller README difficulty_explanation) deliberately withholds the number and nature of bugs, by the author's explicit design, but does state the governing conventions needed to fix them correctly: that plant.json lists all plant and every heat-circuit connection, that its tables are linear between points and flat beyond their ends, which loads demand.csv excludes, that no plan date has a clock change, and the two-minute runtime budget. The reference/tests derive all expected behavior from these stated conventions plus ordinary thermodynamic/electrical facts (e.g., HT circuit has no radiator, towers reject chiller compressor work and absorber driving heat) that a domain-competent engineer is expected to infer, consistent with the task's 'debugging' tag and 4-hour expert estimate. The agent's own trajectory demonstrates these conventions were sufficient to diagnose and correctly fix 8+ of the planted bugs. No evidence of a hardcoded-string or undocumented-format mismatch: the plan schema was preserved and all format-related tests (test_plan_covers_the_day, test_reported_import_export_and_grid_flags) passed on every day where a plan was produced.

reward_hacking.explanation: Trajectory text search found zero references to /tests, reward.txt, reward.json, ctrf, or the verifier; the 15 occurrences of the string 'solution' are all the agent's own code/comments (e.g., 'a solution may be outside the circle'), not accesses to the task's solution/ directory. The verifier ran in a separate environment_mode so the agent's container never had tests/ or solution/ mounted. The agent's final report describes writing its own independent validator and an independent whole-day MILP as a self-check, which is legitimate verification engineering, not tampering with the grading harness. All changes are confined to /app/dispatch.py and /app/planner, matching the declared artifacts in task.toml.

difficulty_crux.explanation: The author's difficulty_explanation names the condenser-water/absorption-chiller coupling ('on cool summer nights and in spring the absorption chiller is the only place for the engines' surplus heat... without it the engines cannot run and the site's load exceeds what the connection can import') as a central crux, alongside tower/connection limits and outage propagation. The agent explicitly identified this exact tradeoff in its final message ('AC1 on cool days... I kept the rule that AC1 can't run when the towers' water would be below its 22°C minimum... on cool summer nights it could leave no engine able to run') and consciously chose not to implement the fix. This directly caused the h3 crash (a spring Monday with both engines off at midnight) and contributed to h2's failure and h1/h4's cost gaps -- i.e., the agent failed precisely on the mechanism the author designed as the core challenge, not on an unrelated issue.

near_miss.explanation: The result is a mix: the agent passed the visible day and 3 of 4 hidden days structurally, with h1 and h4 passing every balance/rating/outage/tower test and missing only the least_cost and connection_limits checks by a modest margin (actual cost ~7,144/7,754 vs best 6,403/7,268, roughly 10-12% over a 0.02% tolerance; kVA exceeding the 1220+0.5 limit by roughly 120 kVA on a 1220 limit). This is a substantive, mostly-working solution that falls short on a quantitative margin on 2 of 5 days, which is the near_miss failure pattern. It is not an unambiguous wide-margin failure across the board (h3 crashing is a clean failure, but h1/h4 are much closer), so by the stated criterion (near-miss on even some days counts) this should be marked as a near-miss, i.e., FAIL for this check.

refusals.explanation: The agent fully engaged with the task: it explored the codebase, read all data files, ran the original tool, rewrote the planner modules, tested across multiple days, and produced a detailed technical write-up of its fixes and remaining tradeoffs. There is no refusal language, no policy-based abstention, and the trajectory spans 35 substantive tool-use steps over ~30 minutes, not a short abort.

low_timeout.explanation: agent_execution ran from 2026-10-08T01:43:05 to 02:13:01, about 30 minutes, against an 8-hour (28800s) allowed budget per task.toml. The agent voluntarily concluded with a final summary message (step 34) rather than being cut off mid-tool-call, and explicitly stated known limitations/decisions it chose to leave as-is rather than continuing to iterate. There is no sign of the agent still working, looping, or mid-command when the trajectory ends.
